shots.text: At Nachat Primary School in Laos, a teacher watches her pupils playing outside.
Her concern is what they might find in the ground.
Years later, she would explain that she had watched the children constantly, afraid they would discover a bomb, and start playing with it.
When clearance teams searched the playground, they found thirty unexploded bombs.
The aircraft that dropped them had disappeared decades earlier.
The children had been born long after the fighting ended.
Yet the war had been waiting for them at school.
Between nineteen sixty-four and nineteen seventy-three, American aircraft dropped more than two million tonnes of ordnance on Laos.
Relative to its population, it became the most heavily bombed country in history.
For people in the worst-hit areas, survival meant reorganising almost every part of life.
Families sheltered underground.
Hospitals operated inside mountains.
Farmers ventured out at night, to work the fields that kept them alive.
But surviving the bombing would leave them with another problem.
Millions of the weapons falling around them did not explode.
To understand how this happened, we need to look beyond Vietnam.
Laos sits immediately to its west, sharing a long border with its larger neighbour.
During the Cold War, that geography placed the country between competing armies and political ambitions.
Laos also had its own struggle for power.
Royalists, neutralists, and the communist Pathet Lao competed for control, with foreign governments supporting different sides.
In nineteen sixty-two, an international agreement promised a way out.
Fourteen countries endorsed the neutrality of Laos.
Foreign military interference was supposed to stop.
On paper, the country would be protected from the surrounding conflict.
On the ground, the agreement failed to produce lasting peace.
North Vietnamese forces continued operating in Laos, and supporting the Pathet Lao.
The United States backed anti-communist forces, including a CIA-supported army whose ranks included many Hmong fighters.
For Washington, losing Laos threatened to strengthen communist power across Southeast Asia.
For North Vietnam, access to Laotian territory helped sustain its war farther south.
The people living between these objectives faced a conflict that neutrality had supposedly prevented.
Through eastern and southern Laos ran parts of the supply network known as the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
It was a shifting system of roads, tracks, and routes, used to move troops and supplies toward the fighting in South Vietnam.
American aircraft attacked this network to disrupt those movements.
Elsewhere, bombing supported the struggle against communist forces inside Laos itself.
For military planners, the landscape contained supply routes, troop positions, and strategic targets.
For the families beneath the aircraft, it contained their homes, their fields, and the paths connecting one village to another.
More than half a million bombing missions were flown over Laos during the campaign.
The often-repeated comparison is a planeload of bombs every eight minutes, around the clock, for nine years.
That is an average across the campaign.
It does not mean every village was struck at regular intervals.
Bombing was concentrated in particular regions, where the experience could be devastating.
A family might survive one attack, and still lose the means to survive the weeks after it.
A ruined house needed rebuilding.
A damaged field still needed planting.
Someone had to find food, collect water, and look after the children.
Waiting for the entire war to end was impossible.
In northeastern Laos, the limestone mountains around Viengxay offered somewhere to hide.
The Pathet Lao established a headquarters in the area.
Leaders, fighters, workers, and civilians used its caves as bombing intensified.
Over time, thousands of people sheltered in and around a dispersed underground settlement.
Caves accommodated government offices, shops, a bakery, a school, and a hospital.
There was even a theatre.
These facilities served a revolutionary stronghold, as well as the people sheltering there.
Political organisation and civilian survival occupied the same landscape.
The mountains allowed activities that had become dangerous above ground to continue beneath it.
A classroom could operate behind rock.
Patients could be treated away from exposed buildings.
Work could continue while aircraft passed overhead.
But there was one essential part of life they could not move inside a mountain.
The fields.
People still needed to grow food.
Shelter offered protection from an air raid, but remaining inside indefinitely meant going hungry.
Survivors described tending crops at night, using darkness to reduce their exposure.
One former resident recalled that going outside also brought relief from caves that became cold and wet.
Even the place keeping them alive could make them ill.
Their routine had been overturned.
Darkness offered a chance to work.
Daylight could mean retreating into shelter, and waiting.
The decision to leave a cave was repeated for ordinary necessities, long before anyone could know when the bombing would stop.
Illness created another dangerous journey.
In the Viengxay oral histories, one resident remembered that seriously sick villagers had to be taken to the provincial hospital at night.
Travelling during the day was too dangerous.
A major cave hospital in the region contained separate wards and operating rooms.
Its interior was fitted to help protect patients from water dripping through the rock.
That detail reveals how much effort survival required.
Finding a cavern was only the beginning.
It had to become somewhere medical staff could work, and patients could recover.
A person might survive the journey to shelter, then face another journey to reach treatment.
The caves preserved lives, but they could not remove every risk outside their entrances.
Beyond the cave settlements, communities faced the consequences of weapons designed to scatter danger across wide areas.
Cluster bombs opened in the air, and released smaller explosive submunitions.
More than two hundred and seventy million of these submunitions were dropped over Laos.
An estimated eighty million failed to detonate.
Those figures describe the scale of the contamination left after the campaign.
They are not a count of everything still remaining today.
But even at the time, the implication was enormous.
An attack could end, without its danger ending.
Small unexploded weapons could remain where people needed to walk, plant, or build.
When the American bombing ended in nineteen seventy-three, people could begin reclaiming activities that aircraft had interrupted.
Yet returning to the land brought them into contact with what the aircraft had left.
A farmer digging into contaminated soil could strike an explosive.
A child could discover an unfamiliar metal object.
A family planning a house could find that the ground beneath it needed investigating first.
The danger changed location.
During the bombing, people had watched the sky.
Afterward, they also had to worry about what lay under their feet.
And the land could not simply be abandoned.
Rural livelihoods depended on using it.
Contamination restricted agriculture and development, creating a cruel relationship between poverty and risk.
People needed productive land, while the explosives made that land dangerous to use.
Scrap metal introduced another temptation.
The remnants of war could be worth money.
For poor households, collecting metal offered income, but searching for it could bring them into direct contact with live ordnance.
The same object could appear to offer a small financial opportunity, and carry the power to destroy a family.
This danger outlasted the generation that had watched the aircraft arrive.
Children encountered weapons without having witnessed the events that put them there.
Explaining the war became part of keeping them safe.
In Phon Village, a father named Atta discovered a small unexploded munition, just metres from where his children played.
He did not know whom to call.
Afraid to leave it exposed, he buried it.
The decision left him with a new fear: that he might strike it again, while planting or building.
When a clearance team arrived in twenty twenty-two, he asked whether they had found it.
They had.
They destroyed it, along with other explosives on his land.
After clearance, his family expanded their garden, planted fruit trees, built storage, and began preparing for a new house.
The transformation was practical.
Land he had worried about could support his children.
The work of ending the war, for that household, involved making its garden usable.
Return now to Nachat Primary School.
Thirty bombs were found in its playground.
For years, a teacher had watched children playing, and wondered what their curiosity might uncover.
After clearance, parents could send their children to school with one less fear.
Decades earlier, people around Viengxay had moved classrooms into caves, to protect children from weapons falling out of the sky.
Their descendants still needed specialists to remove those weapons from the ground.
The history of the bombing is usually measured in missions, tonnage, and targets.
Its civilian history has another set of measurements.
The distance to shelter.
The hours available to work a field.
The journey to a hospital after dark.
The patch of ground a parent will not let a child enter.
People kept teaching, treating the sick, and growing food through years of bombardment.
Afterward, they continued rebuilding around explosives they had never chosen to live beside.
The aircraft stopped coming in nineteen seventy-three.
For families still waiting for their land to be cleared, safety has arrived one field, one garden, and one playground at a time.
